definition: Directing an AI coding agent in plain natural language to build software — describing the outcome you want and reviewing what it produces, instead of typing every line yourself.

The natural-language instructions you type to tell an agent what to do — vibecoding's equivalent of writing code, but in plain English. A good prompt gives enough detail to avoid guessing, without spelling out every line yourself.
A project file (sometimes named AGENTS.md instead) that you write once, upfront, listing your codebase's conventions and rules, so an AI agent doesn't have to guess them fresh on every task.
Repetitive, predictable code every project needs (setup, config, standard structure) that takes no real creative thought to write — exactly the kind of grunt work AI agents handle well.
The exact set of changes — lines added, removed, or edited — an agent made to your code, shown side by side so you can review precisely what changed before accepting it.
When an AI agent states something false as if it were fact — like a function, flag, or API that doesn't actually exist — sounding just as confident as it would if it were right.
When an agent's changes quietly spread beyond what you actually asked for — touching extra files or features you didn't request — which makes the diff harder to trust and review.
A system (like Git) that tracks every change made to your code over time, so you can undo a change or roll back to an earlier state if something goes wrong.
Short for 'repository' — the folder holding a project's entire codebase, tracked by a version control system like Git so every file and its history lives in one place.
A separate, parallel copy of a codebase in version control (like Git) where you can make and test changes without touching the main version — you merge it back in only once you're happy with it.

A saved snapshot of your code's current state in version control, labeled with a short message describing what changed. Committing often — e.g. after every small step — gives you an undo button back to any of those points.
A Git command that overwrites a shared branch's history with your local version, permanently discarding whatever commits were there before — unlike a normal edit, it can't just be undone.
When an agent's grip on the conversation drifts during a long chat, and it starts forgetting or ignoring rules and constraints you set earlier in that same session.
